name: Smedley Butler

summary.text: Smedley Darlington Butler (1881–1940) was a U.S. Marine Corps officer who received two Medals of Honor, for Veracruz, Mexico (1914) and for the attack on Fort Rivière, Haiti (1915), and retired as a major general in 1931. In 1935 he published War Is a Racket and wrote in the magazine Common Sense that he had spent most of his 33 years of active service as "a high-class muscle man for Big Business, for Wall Street and for the bankers." In November 1934 he testified before the House's McCormack–Dickstein committee that bond salesman Gerald C. MacGuire had tried to recruit him to lead a veterans' march on Washington; the committee's February 1935 report stated that the attempts were discussed and planned and might have been placed in execution, but no one was prosecuted.

facts.claim: Butler received two Medals of Honor: the first for the U.S. occupation of Veracruz, Mexico, in April 1914, where his citation credits him with leading his battalion through the action of April 22 and the final occupation of the city; the second for leading the attack on Fort Rivière, Haiti, on November 17, 1915.
facts.quote: The first of Butler's two Medals of Honor was earned during the U.S. occupation of Veracruz, Mexico, in April 1914. ... According to his second citation, Butler led an attack on Fort Riviere on November 17, 1915.

facts.claim: Butler retired from the Marine Corps in 1931 with the rank of major general and died in 1940 at 58; by then he had more decorations than any other Marine.
facts.quote: in 1931, Butler retired from the Marine Corps with the rank of major general.

sources.title: Major Smedley D Butler
Why Smedley Butler Turned Against US Empire

facts.claim: War Is a Racket, first published in 1935, argues that the wars Butler fought in were undertaken for the profit of private commercial interests in the United States.
facts.quote: The author asserts that he personally fought in several wars, which were undertaken exclusively for the profit of private commercial interests in the United States.

sources.title: War Is a Racket, by Smedley D. Butler

facts.claim: In Common Sense, Vol. 4, No. 11 (November 1935), Butler wrote that he had spent 33 years and four months in active service and most of that time as "a high-class muscle man for Big Business, for Wall Street and for the bankers," adding, "In short, I was a racketeer for capitalism."
facts.quote: he spent 33 years and four months in active service and most of his time being a high-class muscle man for Big Business, for Wall Street and for the bankers. ... "In short, I was a racketeer for capitalism."

facts.claim: Butler testified to the McCormack–Dickstein committee in November 1934 that Gerald C. MacGuire had attempted to recruit him to lead a march on Washington with a promised army of 500,000 men and financial backing, in which Butler would hold a new position of "Secretary of General Affairs" while President Roosevelt became a figurehead.
facts.quote: Butler testified that Gerald C. MacGuire attempted to recruit him to lead a coup, promising him an army of 500,000 men for a march on Washington, D.C., and financial backing.

facts.claim: The committee began examining evidence on November 20, 1934, released a statement on its preliminary findings on November 24, 1934, and submitted its final report to the House on February 15, 1935.
facts.quote: On February 15, 1935, the committee submitted its final report to the House of Representatives.

facts.claim: The committee's February 1935 report stated that "there is no question that these attempts were discussed, were planned, and might have been placed in execution" when and if the financial backers deemed it expedient; no one was prosecuted.
facts.quote: there is no question that these attempts were discussed, were planned, and might have been placed in execution

facts.claim: MacGuire, in sworn testimony, denied almost all of Butler's account, frequently answering "Not to my recollection" or "I do not remember," and told reporters he had only visited Butler to sell him bonds and that Butler's testimony was "a publicity stunt." Journalist Paul Comly French, who investigated independently, confirmed Butler's story to the committee.
facts.quote: MacGuire told reporters that he had only gone to see Butler to sell him some bonds and that Butler's testimony was "a publicity stunt." Paul French, a journalist who investigated independently, confirmed Butler's story to the committee.

facts.claim: Butler said the committee had edited out of its published findings the business figures he had named; the committee said it had no evidence before it that would warrant calling such men. Those Butler implicated denied any involvement.
facts.quote: committee has had no evidence before it that would in the slightest degree warrant calling before it such men...

openQuestions: The Crash Conduits page links Butler to DuPont, GM and Prescott Bush; the sources returned caution that names such as J.P. Morgan Jr. and Irénée du Pont appear mainly in popular histories, and the committee did not call them. No connection to those entities is recorded.
The committee report's official House document number was not confirmed.
Dates for the preliminary statement differ (November 24 vs. November 26, 1934).
